source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Gap 2. Wason 2-4-6 rule discovery adapted for 11 LLMs. Models mostly test triples that fit their current guess instead of ones that could refute it. Models with long reasoning traces show less of this and succeed more.
numbers: 11 LLMs (Qwen3 8B/14B/32B, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, QwQ-32B, R1-Distill-Llama-70B); task success from 6% to 78% within 45 turns; 80 episodes per model-variant; confirmation bias measured as ratio of incompatible to compatible tests (I:C); higher I:C goes with higher success.
quote: LLMs exhibit confirmation bias, often proposing triples to confirm their hypothesis rather than trying to falsify it.
limits: Toy numeric rule task, not case selection. Later human work says positive tests are not always biased; the paper follows Wason's design anyway.
agent_relevance: First measured rate of confirm-first testing in LLMs. Supports a 'seek the refuting case' step when the agent picks cases, but transfer from number triples to historical cases is untested.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, intervention results
finding: Gap 2. Two human debiasing prompts (Dual-Goal, Think-in-Opposites) raise I:C and success. Effect is significant for thinking-mode models but mixed for non-thinking models.
numbers: Average rule discovery 42% to 56% with interventions (abstract). Dual-Goal raised success in 8 of 11 models. Example thinking-mode I:C: Qwen3-32B 0.14 baseline, 0.54 TiO, 0.77 Dual-Goal. Non-thinking Qwen3-14B and 32B: Dual-Goal success fell (0.23 to 0.13; 0.33 to 0.10). Human Wason baseline: 29 participants, 21 found the rule, I:C 1.79 if right first time versus 0.24 if not.
limits: Table layout read from pdftotext, so single cells may be misaligned. Prompt gain is task-specific; distilled version generalised to Blicket test and math self-correction per authors.
agent_relevance: A 'seek the case that would refute' rule is cheap and measured to help on a hypothesis-testing task, but can backfire on small non-thinking models. Test it by model size.

source: McAllister (2018) Using History as Evidence in Philosophy of Science: A Methodological Critique, J. Philosophy of History 12:239-258
finding: Gap 3. Describes the Virginia Tech 'Testing Theories of Scientific Change' project. About 250 hypotheses from Kuhn, Feyerabend, Lakatos and Laudan were collated; 32 were sent out for testing as 'case studies' (Donovan, Laudan, Laudan 1988). McAllister lists five flaws.
numbers: 250 hypotheses collated, 32 tested. Example test: Perrin tested thesis GA4.5 on 69 chemists (age in 1785 versus age at adopting oxygen theory) and judged it disconfirmed. Five criticisms: claims are quantitative so need cross-case statistics; quantitative methods misread; case studies not separated from quasi-experiments; items are not real case studies; hypothesis generation confused with test.
quote: Although case studies are in principle sufficient to refute a general thesis, in practice they rarely do so. (Hull, quoted)
limits: Secondary critique by one author. Laudan and Laudan themselves later describe the project's 'limited impact'. No pooled effect size or coder agreement is reported in this source; those remain unfound.
agent_relevance: The best-resourced attempt to test methodology theories on many cases got no clean verdict. Rule: a case test needs a stated quantitative claim, a defined population and a test that could fail.

source: McAllister (2018), account of Hull, Tessner and Diamond (1978) Planck's Principle, Science 202:717-723
finding: Gap 6. The founding quantitative test of Planck's principle on 67 British scientists after Darwin's Origin (1859). Those who accepted evolution by 1869 were younger on average, but age explained little.
numbers: 67 scientists born before 1839 and alive in 1869. Mean age in 1859: 39.6 (accepted by 1869) versus 48.1 (not accepted), significant. Age explained under 10% of variance. Among those who accepted, older ones were as quick as younger ones. Verdict: principle disconfirmed on balance.
limits: Read via McAllister's summary, not the Science paper. One episode (Darwin in Britain). Later tests (Perrin, 69 French chemists on oxygen theory, disconfirmed; Wray 2003; Sulloway 2014) cited only by title.
agent_relevance: Shows how a famous case claim looks after a population test: direction right, size small. Agent should report effect size, not just direction, when a claim rests on an iconic case.

source: McAllister (2018), section on testing scientific realism
finding: Gap 10 (partial). Case-based arguments on the pessimistic meta-induction are attacked on sample grounds: Psillos says the inductive base is not big or representative; Fahrbach says Laudan's examples come from the earliest 10% of scientific work; Mizrahi says fewer theories were abandoned than assumed. McAllister says the right test is a correlation across a broad population of theories.
numbers: No stabilisation threshold is given. Only the 10% (Fahrbach, citing Price's exponential growth) is numeric.
limits: Argument, not data. Gap 10 (how many cases) stays unanswered in numbers.
agent_relevance: If the agent's cases all come from one era or field, it should say the sample covers a small, unrepresentative slice.

source: Cheng and Weinberg (2024) Old and Connected versus Young and Creative: Networks and the Diffusion of New Scientific Ideas, NBER w33030
finding: Gap 6. A new large-sample test in the Planck family (biomedical research, NLP plus network fixed effects). Adoption of new ideas is hump-shaped in innovator career age: young innovators win at short network distance, mid-career innovators at long distance.
numbers: Abstract and front matter read; simulations say aging of innovators and of adopters have comparable effects on adoption. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Biomedicine only. Working paper. Young adopters being open is the Planck mechanism, but the effect depends on network distance.
agent_relevance: Planck's principle now has a nuanced, field-bounded result. Treat the 'old guard resists' story as a conditional claim.

source: Goodstein (2000) In Defense of Robert Andrews Millikan, Engineering and Science 63(4):30-38
finding: Gap 6. Test case for 'selective data' charges. Millikan's 1913 paper reported 58 oil drops and said they were all drops over 60 days. Notebooks hold more. Goodstein argues the selection was legitimate and that Franklin's re-analysis shows almost no change in the result.
numbers: Published 58 drops; notebooks show about 100 drops in the 63 days (about 25 aborted, about 75 complete) per Goodstein; the accusers count about 175 drops from 11 Nov 1911 to 16 Apr 1912. Claimed uncertainty 0.2%, about 15 times better than earlier work. Franklin: using all data would barely change e or its error.
limits: Defence essay by a Caltech physicist with an interest. The two drop counts (100 vs 175) differ by time window and counting rule. Not an independent audit.
agent_relevance: A usable source-check test case: the paper text says 'all drops' while the notebook says otherwise, yet the effect on the result is small. Agent should separate 'claim false' from 'claim consequential'.

source: Pires and Branco (2010) A Statistical Model to Explain the Mendel-Fisher Controversy, Statistical Science 25(4):545-565
finding: Gap 6. Fisher (1936) found Mendel's data fit too well. Franklin et al. (2008) dropped most of Fisher's other points but conceded 'too good to be true' stands. Pires and Branco give a model of unconscious bias that reproduces the too-good fit without fraud.
numbers: Fisher's pooled chi-square p-value about 0.99993 (about 7 in 100,000 chance of a fit this close). Method: recomputed chi-squares, Monte Carlo, meta-analysis of p-values, minimum distance estimates.
quote: There are reasonable grounds to assume that a certain unconscious bias was systematically introduced in Mendel's experimentation.
limits: A model that fits, not a proof; the controversy is not closed. Franklin 2008 book was not opened.
agent_relevance: Good test case for an agent's reading of 'too good' data: it should list fraud, bias and selection as live explanations instead of picking one from the story.

source: Lu et al. (2026) Empirical-MCTS: Continuous Agent Evolution via Dual-Experience Monte Carlo Tree Search
finding: Gap 4. Experience memory plus search beats repeated sampling on AIME25, but the gain comes with the evolving prompt, not memory alone.
numbers: AIME25 (30 problems, so 1 problem = 3.3 points). Table 1 on DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus: baseline 56.7, ICL 53.3, ReAct 60.0, FLEX 66.6, repeated sampling 70.0, LLaMA-Berry 63.3, theirs 73.3. Ablation with gpt-oss-120b: full method 63.3 to 76.7 at 8 rollouts as experiences grew 110 to 311; without PE-EMP and memory 56.7; repeated sampling plateaus 56.7 after 2 rollouts; without meta-prompt diminishing returns after 240 experiences. MathArena Apex: 2.08 and 4.17 vs 0.00.
limits: Two backbones mixed in the text. Single seed, 30 problems. Token-cost matching is not shown in the extracted text; a cost plot exists.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 4: memory plus search beats repeats, but the equal-token claim is not proved here. Keep an equal-attempt control in any test.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Decocted Experience Improves Test-Time Inference in LLM Agents
finding: Gap 4. Distilled lessons beat raw stored trajectories, more retrieved examples can hurt, and mid-size consolidated memory can beat full memory. Tested on math, web browsing and software engineering under a fixed test-time budget.
numbers: Full-memory sizes in figure 4: 14k, 1.3k, 579 items; k-means consolidation has a sweet spot at intermediate sizes. As retrieved K rises, raw-experience performance can degrade (noisy demonstrations); distilled lessons help most on WebShop.
limits: Exact accuracy numbers were not extracted from the figures. One group.
agent_relevance: Supports a small, distilled case set (consistent with Sourati's one best case) over dumping many cases. Optimal count depends on the task; no universal N.

source: Pan and Zhao (2025) Can Past Experience Accelerate LLM Reasoning? (SpeedupLLM)
finding: Gap 4. Past experience in memory lets LLMs reach answers with less compute, depending on how similar earlier questions are and which memory and reasoning method is used.
numbers: Up to 56% lower compute cost with in-context memory plus DFS reasoning at the highest similarity level (S3); the speedup holds in 64 of 80 settings (80 from the search summary; 56% confirmed in text).
limits: Baseline is no memory, not repeated attempts. High similarity levels are close to repeated questions.
agent_relevance: Case memory saves tokens mainly when cases closely resemble the new task; far analogies are the weak spot, and HPS cases are far analogies.

source: Gao et al. (2026) Can LLMs Act as Historians? ProHist-Bench via the Chinese Imperial Examination
finding: Gap 8. A historian-built benchmark with per-question rubrics, scored by an LLM judge picked after checking six candidate judges against historians. Top models score about 30 of 100.
numbers: 400 questions, 10,891 rubric criteria, 8 dynasties, 18 LLMs, 125 source papers; six historians wrote 100 questions each with at least two-person review. Judge check: 50 sampled instances, historians marked each rubric item 0/1; DeepSeek-R1 had the highest average Pearson correlation 0.77 at both answer and rubric level. Best Rubric Scores near 30 (Gemini-3-Pro about 32 in one setting).
limits: Chinese history, facts and rubric hits, not analysis of method or case use. 0.77 on 50 items from one team; no kappa. Not a test of case-as-evidence judgement.
agent_relevance: Partial close of gap 8: a rubric judge can reach r about 0.77 with historians on fact-and-argument rubrics. For HPS cases a custom rubric and a similar 50-item check would be the template.

source: Bazigaran and Sohn (2025) Concept Generalization in Humans and Large Language Models: Insights from the Number Game
finding: Gap 1 (nearby). Humans generalise from one example; LLMs needed more examples and leaned on rules. So LLMs are not obviously prone to hasty generalisation from very few items in this task.
numbers: GPT does not generalise beyond a single example; GPT-4o-mini showed some; also tested GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-3-8B.
limits: Number concepts, not claims about history. Different from asserting a conclusion from a few anecdotes in prose.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the LLM over-generalises from few cases. Measure it on narrative claims first.

source: Xiong (2026) Language models lack systematicity in generating and updating hypotheses
finding: Gap 1 (nearby). Eight open LLMs on the number game. They favour narrower hypotheses than humans, and as examples accumulate their accuracy declines while confidence grows. Thinking mode reduces or reverses the gap and lowers confidence.
numbers: Eight LLMs (Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5/3.6 and others); three tasks (prediction, evaluation, generation) compared with a Bayesian model and human data.
quote: As examples accumulate, their accuracy declines while their confidence grows.
limits: Number game only. Open models. Exact effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Direct warning for case-counting rules: more cases can raise confidence without raising accuracy. Cap stated confidence by the quality of cases, not their count.

source: Hla (2026) Machina Mirabilis / GPT-1900 (3.3B model trained on pre-1900 text), via blog and press summaries
finding: Gap 7. Closest thing found to an LLM rediscovery test of a historical discovery from period-only text. Mostly failed; one output echoed Planck's 'definite quantities of energy'.
numbers: About 22B tokens pretraining, about 2,600 physics texts midtraining; tests: ultraviolet catastrophe, photoelectric effect, special and general relativity. No scored rate in the snippets.
limits: Seen only through search summaries; not the primary page. No arXiv paper; no comparison to historians' accounts.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open for measured results. Treat as an anecdote until a scored version exists.

source: Underwood, Nelson, Wilkens (2025) Can Language Models Represent the Past without Anachronism?
finding: Gap 7. Prompting a modern model with period prose does not give period-consistent text. Fine-tuning fooled an automated judge but not human readers; pretraining on period text may be needed.
limits: Search summary only. About style, not discovery.
agent_relevance: A modern model cannot be trusted to play a period scientist from a prompt. Rediscovery tests need time-locked models.

source: Valleriani et al. (via Science News, 2026) AI analysis of 76,000 sixteenth-century textbook pages
finding: Gap 9 (nearby). Historians using computation on a large corpus stress that surviving data are incomplete and that choosing a subset is a decision AI cannot undo.
limits: Press report from a search summary. Not a test of Herfeld's rule.
agent_relevance: Supports Herfeld's call for explicit, repeatable selection; no measured comparison of rule versus free choice was found.
